title: History at Home
sub: Grades 3–4 · Who Gets Remembered? · An everyday life as history
objective: Students will learn how Women’s History Month began and use numbers from the *Who Gets Remembered?* room to see that only three of the fifty people with the most monuments in the United States are women. They will then meet Violet Dina Want, a working woman born in London in 1907, and read her family photographs and biography as evidence of everyday life, to explain why an ordinary woman’s life is part of history.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: History is not only the people with statues. Everyday lives, like Violet’s, show how people really lived, and every family has stories worth keeping.

materials: *Who Gets Remembered?* and *Violet’s Life* on a screen, or page 3 of this plan
questions: Whose statues, plaques or street names are there where you live? Who chose them?
What can these photographs tell us about Violet’s life? What can’t they?
Violet left school at 14 to help her family. What does that tell us about life for working families then?
Whose stories are missing from the history you learn, and how could we find them?

steps.title: Who gets a statue?
script: Open *Who Gets Remembered?* on the screen (or read from page 3). *“These are the 50 people with the most public monuments in the United States. How many do you think are women?”* Every student writes a guess. Use the room’s slider for the class’s guess, then uncover the names.

screen.alt: The Who Gets Remembered? room: rows of statue figures, a few of them orange, beside a question and a guess
screen.caption: These are the 50 people with the most public monuments in the United States. How many do you think are women?

steps.purpose: Guess before knowing: let the number surprise them.
students: Make a guess: how many of the 50 are women?

steps.title: Only three
script: Only **three** are women: Joan of Arc, Harriet Tubman and Sacagawea. Ask the room’s own question: *“Why might so few women have monuments?”* Take answers; don’t settle it yet.

screen.text:
Only 3 of the 50 are women.
Joan of Arc · Harriet Tubman · Sacagawea

steps.purpose: Reveal the answer, and ask why.
students: Why might so few women have monuments?

steps.title: How the month began
script: **The month.** Poster 1 tells it: Women’s History Month began in **1978** as a week-long celebration in Santa Rosa, California. In **1980** President Jimmy Carter declared the first National Women’s History Week, and by **1987** Congress expanded it to the whole month of March. The poster gives the reason: *“Historically, women’s roles have often been overshadowed by those of men, who were traditionally credited with “shaping history.””*

screen.caption: How Women’s History Month began, as poster 1 tells it

cells: A week-long celebration begins in Santa Rosa, California.
President Jimmy Carter declares the first National Women’s History Week.
Congress expands it to the whole month of March.
Women’s History Month honors the achievements and contributions of women.

steps.purpose: Give the month its history: a week in one town that grew into a national month.
students: How many years from the first week to the whole month?

steps.title: Meet Violet
script: **A life.** Show the four photographs from poster 2 before telling anything. *“What can a photograph tell us? What can’t it?”* Then tell Violet’s life from the poster: born in London in 1907 into a big working-class family; her father a hotel doorman who sometimes brought home leftover food; top of her class, with teachers who hoped she would teach; leaving school at 14 to work as a machinist, paid for each piece she finished, because her family needed the money; married in 1928; four children, kept warm in coats she cut down and re-sewed; a piano she played by ear; after the war, a corner house in Essex with roses at the bottom of the garden; and later, work at the greengrocer’s.

steps.title: Everyday history
script: **The big idea.** Read the poster’s last lines, on screen. Poster 1 says the same: history is told *“not just through the contributions of overlooked inventors, activists, artists, and writers, but also through the everyday lives of ordinary women.”*

screen.text: The personal histories of women like her help us understand the past—not just in grand historical events, but through the everyday sacrifices and triumphs of ordinary people who shaped the world we live in today.
screen.cite: Poster 2 · Biography of a Working Class Woman

steps.purpose: Name the big idea: ordinary lives are history too.
students: What does Violet’s life tell us that a statue can’t?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels use the same statue numbers and the same story of Violet’s life.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Color the three women among fifty statues, read a family photograph with a checklist, number four moments of Violet’s life, and finish *Violet’s story is history too, because…*

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Fill in how Women’s History Month began, work out the statue numbers, read four details of Violet’s life as evidence of everyday life, and explain poster 1’s big idea.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh four facts as evidence for poster 1’s claim, compare what a statue and a family biography remember, and plan a monument to a woman in their own life.

steps.purpose: Read the numbers and the evidence at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three look at who gets remembered, and at Violet’s life as evidence.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; ask one student to answer each aloud, and a Red Level student the last.

steps.title: A monument of your own
script: Close with the room’s last question: *“If you could raise a monument to one woman in your life or your community, who would it be, and why?”*
